metadata.title: Teacher support for student learning: Insights from PISA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD policy paper uses PISA 2022 micro-data covering 81 countries and economies, with results reported as estimates from complex samples rather than census values. The report’s Reader’s Guide specifies that school principal responses are weighted so that they are proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in the school when school-level information is presented. For student-level indicators (e.g., teacher support indices and percentages), the paper emphasizes statistical uncertainty (standard errors and confidence intervals) and significance testing, consistent with PISA’s complex sampling design, but it does not name specific student weight variables in the provided text. Because this is a descriptive/correlational policy synthesis rather than an ML modeling paper, the manuscript does not document replicate-weight procedures or explicit student weight variable names; analysts should rely on the PISA technical documentation for the exact weight and variance-estimation variables.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable here because the report focuses on teacher support indices and questionnaire-based measures (e.g., TEACHSUP and related practice indicators) and on descriptive/correlational relationships rather than reporting an achievement outcome derived from PV-based cognitive scales in the provided excerpt. Missing-data handling is not reported in the excerpt because the paper instead uses PISA publication conventions (e.g., symbols for missing/insufficient observations) and notes that some entities had sampling-standard issues due to COVID-19, without specifying an imputation or deletion rule for missing questionnaire responses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report uses PISA 2022 student questionnaire data for 15-year-olds in mathematics lessons to measure teacher support, and it also uses PISA 2012 and 2003 for trend analyses of the same four teacher-support items in mathematics. It reports that PISA 2022 results include data from all participating education systems even when some sampling standards were not met due to COVID-19, with annotated caution for specific entities. For teacher-level analyses, it relies on the optional PISA 2022 teacher questionnaire and notes that due to missing data the findings are based on input from 11 to 16 of the 18 available countries/economies. The excerpt does not specify additional student-level inclusion/exclusion rules beyond the PISA target population definition and the publication conventions for missing/insufficient observations (e.g., fewer than 30 students or fewer than 5 schools with valid data).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD policy paper synthesizes PISA evidence on teacher support for student learning, focusing on mathematics lessons in PISA 2022 and using earlier cycles (2003 and 2012) to describe trends up to 2022. Teacher support is measured from student questionnaire responses to four items (interest in every student’s learning, extra help when needed, help with learning, and continuing until students understand), combined into the TEACHSUP index (standardized to mean 0 and SD 1 across OECD countries). The report also examines how teacher support varies within versus between schools (with most variation occurring within schools) and relates teacher support to school learning environment factors (student-teacher relationships, disciplinary climate, and student persistence) and to teacher characteristics from the optional teacher questionnaire (time/work-life balance, job satisfaction, and adaptive instruction). It reports correlational associations and statistically significant differences, but explicitly notes that PISA data do not provide causal evidence for the policy interventions discussed. Due to COVID-19-related data collection challenges, some education systems are annotated for sampling-standard concerns, and the report uses confidence intervals and significance testing conventions to guide interpretation.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is treated as a framework/policy synthesis rather than an empirical ML study: the provided text does not describe any predictive modeling pipeline, algorithmic training, or ML evaluation metrics. Consequently, fields related to ML techniques and structured predictive findings are intentionally left empty. The report does provide methodological guidance on PISA coverage, uncertainty, and publication conventions (e.g., handling of insufficient observations and annotated sampling-standard issues), which supports interpretation even though it does not supply the granular ML/PV/missing-data procedures required for an empirical ML extraction.
